messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Looking at the additive effects of 3 QTLs
parts:
Hi Dantee, 

If I understand you correctly and you already know your QTL of interest, then you can use makeqtl() and fitqtl() to fit your loci to a 3 QTL additive model.

If you expect epistatic interactions between QTL you could go through with model selection (e.g. stepwiseqtl() as described in Manichaikul et al. (2009)).

I don't know of a three-dimensional genome scan implementation (I think it would be too computationally expensive), but maybe somebody else can weigh in. 

Sandra Truong

On Tue, Mar 24, 2015 at 9:57 AM, <dantee....@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi,

I was wondering, is there an equivalent of scantwo function in R/qtl, but for examining 3 QTL. I have 3 QTL on three separate chromosomes, and would like to see whether all 3 QTL have additive effects on my phenotype of interest.

Thanks,
Dantee

parts: > I don't know of a three-dimensional genome scan implementation (I think it would be too computationally expensive), but maybe somebody else can weigh in.

There's a function scanqtl() that can be used for higher-order scans; the hard part is making sense of the results. I've never tried to perform a 3-d scan; if you're just looking for additive effects and the loci are on different chromosomes, the single-dimensional scan are likely to be sufficient.

karl
